🗒️What This Means For You
  • Fed Hike: Since the 2026-09-16 Fed hike the Treasury-rate leg of IG returns is -0.46% (intraday, 7-year +6bp). At trading day 21 (last close) it was -0.08% against a five-campaign average of -1.33% at the same point — 1994-95, 1999-00, 2022-23 were worse. The spread leg adds -0.42%. The 10-year is +9bp since the hike vs a +17bp campaign average at the same point. The 2s10s steepening may be topping (intraday 3 of 4 signals: topping likely).
  • HY Contagion: Junk-bond stress: the CCC-to-single-B spread gap is 724bp against a five-year average of 412bp (widest since Apr 2020). Better-rated junk is following: single-B +50bp and BB +43bp in a month. CCC and single-B are moving together more (correlation 0.30 → 0.58 over 3 months; five-year norm 0.70). Investment grade is untouched (+6bp).
  • Bank Earnings: 8 banks reported (FFIN, INDB, SFNC, WAFD, CFG, MTB, RF, TFC); 5 red-flagged (INDB: NPLs +21% QoQ; SFNC: Coverage falling while NPLs rise (+9%, +$14mm); WAFD: NCO ratio +75bp QoQ …). Credit deteriorating at the margin; deposit costs flat. Watch: INDB, SFNC, WAFD, MTB, TFC.
  • Stocks: US stocks closed higher; this morning S&P futures edge up, Nasdaq futures dip.
  • FX: Dollar slips a little; euro and pound firm, yen barely moves near 158.
  • Technicals: S&P and Nasdaq sit just above their 50-day averages, stretched versus history.
  • Sectors: Defensive health care and staples lead this week; tech lags after a big year.
  • Credit/Spreads: Safe corporate bonds look calm, but the riskiest junk bonds are under real strain.
  • Crisis: Overall system stress is moderate; war, oil and high yields are the pressure points.
  • Inflation: Core inflation is steady, but fast-rising prices are spreading through more items.
  • Tech Bubble: Prices look rich and the economy late-cycle, but tech isn't at 2000-style mania.
  • Earnings & IPOs: Meta is the giant reporting next week; Bloom Energy could swing hardest.
  • Iran: The war grinds on: ships hit near Hormuz, talks stalled, oil stays high.
  • Warsh: Fed chair gave no rate hint; Street expects October pause, December hike.
  • Outlook: Near term neutral; rising bond yields and junk-bond stress cap the upside.
  • Trades: Favor quality credit over junk, health care over tech, wait on gold.
  • Trades Vol: 45 watchlist names screened: 2 buy, 1 sell, 21 hold long, 21 stay out
  • Pre-market: Twelve gappers, zero catalysts, zero names cleared either rule set, so both watchlists are empty and the honest trade is no trade. Also, the data itself looks stale for a premarket scan (see the data note below), so treat every gap number with suspicion.
  • Treasury Liquidity: Treasury liquidity/rates-vol monitor: TLT 95/100 put skew +0.54 vol pts, Fed DKW real term premium +91bp.
  • 10Y Pattern: 10Y at 93th pctile, +19bp from the 2026 rim — still compressing, not a cup-and-handle.
  • Diesel Futures: Diesel: 1-9 of 10 signals point lower.
  • Bottom line: Stocks are calm, but bonds and the riskiest borrowers are flashing caution.

The biggest story this morning is in bonds, not stocks. The US 10Y is up 5.23bp to 5.1103% and the 30Y is at 5.4452%. The 10Y sits 13.39% above its 200DMA, at the 99th percentile (z 2.02, computed). Yields are also rising abroad: JGB 10Y +3bp to 2.93%, Bund +1.6bp to 3.429%. At the last cash close, US equities shrugged this off: S&P 500 +0.33% to 7744.06, Dow +1.08%, Russell 2000 +1.38%, Nasdaq only +0.08%. Pre-market futures are split: ES +0.13%, NQ -0.28%, so the rotation out of tech continues. Europe is firmer (Euro Stoxx 50 +0.70%) and VIX is down to 15.98. Fed chair Warsh, speaking in Bangkok, gave no rate signal for the Oct 27–28 FOMC (CNBC, WaPo). Goldman reads this as an October pause and a final hike in December. Under the calm surface, the junk-bond market is cracking at the bottom rung. The Caa–B spread gap is 724bp, at the 99.9th percentile of its 5-year range and the widest since April 2020. Caa OAS is 1034bp, up 133bp in a month. The stress is starting to climb the ladder: single-B OAS is +50bp in a month to 310bp and Ba is +43bp to 194bp. The 63-day Caa/B correlation has risen to 0.58 from 0.30 three months ago, though it is still below its 0.70 5-year median. So contagion is building but is not yet fully synchronised. IG has barely moved (83bp, +6bp in a month), and the headline HY index OAS of 3.21% still sits at only the 21st percentile. This is a descriptive read, not a validated signal. On sentiment, equities are complacent while rates and lower-quality credit are tightening financial conditions from below. Iran-related shipping attacks keep Brent at $105.87.

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 50th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +91bp.

Latest reading is +0.54 vol points (9th percentile of the 44 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.53 (50th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), improving over the past 3 months (-0.08 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.50pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +91bp (96th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 12bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +14bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 102.5 (74th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 86bp (steeper by 12bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 76% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (105bp above today).
Retracement = (right rim − cup base) / (left rim − cup base) = (5.30 − 0.51) / (6.79 − 0.51) = 76%.
Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base) = 0.51 + 0.90 × (6.79 − 0.51) = 6.16%.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

⚠ Commentary is 15 days old (as of 2026-10-01); it may not reflect the latest Fed news.

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

Curated summary of published Fed, market and economist commentary (news and research via the web), not a computed series and not a forecast. Odds differ by venue and move daily.

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 63/100 — Core trend is sticky-but-contained; breadth of fast-rising prices is the problem. The trimmed/median measures (Median CPI 2.61%, Median PCE 2.57%, Trimmed-Mean PCE 2.19%) are flat-to-falling, but the computed core-trend percentiles sit above the historical middle and Core PCE is 3.00759%. The Dallas distribution shows 28.9% of the PCE basket rising faster than 5% (13.2% >10%, 15.7% at 5–10%). Flexible CPI is 6.12% and rising (82nd pct). Energy pass-through from the war is broadening rather than fading. That keeps the Fed in hold-with-hike-bias mode, not easing.

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (42x) ≈ 24% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

The current cycle, anchored at Oct-2022, has run 48 months to an index of 243.1. The dot-com analogue anchored at the 1990 bear-market low peaked at month 113 at 1423.9, and the 1994-anchored path peaked at month 69 at 665.3. On either template, today's run is mid-cycle in duration and far smaller in magnitude. The dot-com bust ultimately fell -78.0% over 31 months from its 2000-03-10 peak. What makes 2026 different is concentration and the rates backdrop. The top-10 weight is ~35–40% by published estimates, versus ~25% in 2000 (UBS, via Fool), while the 10Y is above 5% and the Fed is hiking. In 2000, the catalyst was Fed tightening plus a tight-credit-to-wide-credit turn. Today credit is tight at the top but widening at the bottom (CCC). That echoes 1998–2000, when HY deteriorated well before the equity peak. Bottom line: valuation risk is high, but froth is concentrated in mega-caps rather than broad speculative IPO mania. The IPO pipeline is thin this week, and AAII is net bearish. Analyst estimates: CAPE ~41 (GuruFocus 41.15 as of Oct-1), Buffett indicator ~236% (published range 234–237%), and top-10 ~38% (midpoint of conflicting 35–40% reports). The ipo_froth and lt_eps_growth figures are judgment-based estimates, not sourced figures.

These are the most recent reports I could verify, dated Oct 14–15; I could not confirm anything from Oct 16 itself. Diplomacy is stalled. Trump told the UN he is deciding whether to make a deal or drive Iran "into hell." Iran called the US response "insufficient," and Trump says he has "offered them NOTHING" while talks run through mediators (Fox News live, Oct 15). Trump ruled out a nuclear strike, said the war would "end very quickly" after the midterms, and said there are no plans for US ground troops. The Pentagon is reportedly weighing heavy conventional options against nuclear and energy sites. On shipping, one report counts ten attacks on ships this week, and a container ship sank near the Strait of Hormuz after being struck. Oil prices jumped after an attack on Saudi Aramco's headquarters. A projectile hit a Riyadh airport terminal a day after a missile attack killed 13 (Fox News live, Oct 14). Iranian forces have reportedly downed at least two US MQ-1 drones. Qatar condemned Iranian attacks and called for Hormuz to reopen without conditions (CBS/NBC hubs). Market read: Brent $105.87 and Flexible CPI at 6.12% embed a durable risk premium. A post-midterm de-escalation is the main upside catalyst; a Hormuz closure is the tail risk.

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

Oct 27–28 FOMC: most likely a hold. This is my inference from his Oct 16 refusal to prejudge and Goldman's read that the FOMC is set to pause in October. Risk skews hawkish, given the 3.7% September CPI and his comment that events have broadly matched the September projections, which included another hike.

~1 YEAR

Inference from his on-record emphasis on price stability and his 'synchronous tightening, no free riders' framing: likely one more 25bp hike, probably in December (Goldman's base case), from the ~3.9% level set in September. That would be followed by an extended hold through much of 2027. Cuts would come only if the labor market cracks; payrolls are already just 29k. Balance-sheet shrinkage would be a preferred lever over additional hikes, consistent with his long-standing writings. This is my inference, not something he has stated.

At the IMF-World Bank meetings in Bangkok on Oct 16, Warsh pledged price stability as the key. He declined to signal the next move and named October and December as the 'crystallising moments' to judge output, jobs and inflation. He praised a global 'synchronous tightening' with 'no free riders' and called the AI development path 'very bumpy.' The Fed hiked 25bp to ~3.9% in September, its first increase in three years. The 2Y at 4.7571% is pricing at least one more hike. Today's 10Y move to 5.1103% shows the market charging more to hold long-dated bonds, consistent with a hawkish-hold reading.

Sources: CNBC — Fed's Warsh withholds rate signal, praises global tightening (Oct 16) · investingLive — Warsh names October and December as decision points · Washington Post — Warsh says price stability is key · NBC News — Warsh focused on taming rising prices · US News/AP — Warsh shies away from rate signals
